title: AI did over 200 000 playthroughs of my planned game mode
author: s22stumarket
selftext:
Maybe something logical for experienced game devs but I as a beginner felt I discovered something important and useful.

I am planning to add a career mode to my game and before starting to really create and code it, I asked AI to run some simulations. We had already planned different aspects of this game mode together but I wanted to test out the functionalities, end results etc. 

My biggest fear is that somehow some choices will end up the only ways to beat the game and the players would feel obligated to play via one foolproof route. But the goal is that the player can choose the character type they like and that their choices would matter. Also I want to rule out some tricks and XP farming solutions that would otherwise break the game. 

  
So, Claude at first ran about 28 000 simulations, then gave me a list of issues to address. After that ran about 50 000 simulations, we tweaked the findings. After 5 simulation rounds the total is over 200 000. It took into account differenet choices the player can make, different playstyles, skill levels and so on. 

Of course, the final iteration would be the sum of simulations and real play throughs from me and test players. Real human feeling is not something you can simulate. 

So, just a tip and an idea from me on how to use the AI besides coding and creating assets.

comments.author: jildos_legoplanet
comments.body: I would be careful taking any so-whats from a simulated run. AI cannot determine what constitutes good enough. It will keep tweaking as long as you ask it to. Let AI be your resource. Not your director

Good. Just remember that AI cannot experience. It can do QA, find obvious flaws, etc.

It won't know fun.

replies.author: s22stumarket
replies.body:
Of course. The goal is not to simulate fun or feeling.   
One goal is to find (mathematical) and logical flaws in the game. AI for example noticed that if the player is a beginner and has low skills then they fill fall behind and would not reach the endgame and won't event know why. One solutions is that the game (do not have to) will recommend some options and counter-measures which depends on the difficulty. If the player chooses casual mode then the counter-measures to mitigate low skills are stronger, in hard mode they are almost non-existant.

replies.author: egonosz
replies.body: Can you give me an example of how player cannot reach reach the end game. I am just curious.

replies.author: thecircus
replies.body: I guess you could think of it like - How many coins does a player get from defeating an enemy? Is it enough to afford an item in the shop they visit in the next area. Extrapolate this out to many different mechanics and you can have some quite complex data analysis questions answered. Saves some grunt work on doing manual calculations.

replies.author: s22stumarket
replies.body:
Two examples.
The goal in my game is to reach the Grand Tournament. The player has several seasons where they can try to achieve it. But if the skill level is low the player won't ever reach it. So one solution is to gradually lower the requirements in each season.
Other one is about having a DNF in some tournaments. If the DNF will lower XP and loot and raise the risk of further DNF-s then the player can fall into downward spiral.

comments.author: ComputerTraining9274
comments.body:
Not sure what engine or stack you’re using, but another good thing to do is have AI write unit and regression tests. End to end simulations like you have are great for integration testing but I’ve found having concise unit and regression tests helps catch bugs early when adding new features.

Just be careful through cause at least with Claude I’ve found it loves writing some pointless tests too 🤣

comments.author: Arkenhammer
comments.body:
So we tried using ChatGPT to play test our game. It was... not useful. It played at a beginner level but made decidedly non-human mistakes.

It's an interesting question what kind of useful information we could get from a test like that. The biggest thing we are looking for is places where humans misunderstand the UI or the rules of the game. No kind of automated testing will give us that; particularly because we had to create a special rig so ChatGPT could play. However the other thing we are looking for is how our mechanics break at high levels of play. For that we really want the equivalent of Stockfish rather than an LLM. Is it worth building such a thing? Maaaaybe.
